verdicts.why: Plugging into an outlet is a plain physical action with no attitude toward it.
A scheduled transport connection is described flatly; nothing is judged.
Hitting a ball successfully is a plain sporting description; the success is the meaning, not an attitude.
Landing a blow solidly is neutral description of contact, with no side taken.
Presiding over a trial is a plain legal act; the word does not judge the parties.
Deciding a competition's result is a neutral function word with no attitude.
Back-and-forth motion, as in shaking a head, is plain physical description.
Moving with a tremor names the motion without approving or disparaging it.
Sideways or back-and-forth movement is neutral description.
Disturbing someone's peace is a strong meaning, as in 'spirits greatly shaken', but the word carries no attitude beyond it.
Bringing to a condition by shaking, as in 'shake off her gravity', describes a change without judging it.
Rapid vibration is plain physical description with no evaluative load.
Spoken communication is named flatly; any scorn in the sentences comes from the surrounding words, not this one.
A person's manner of speaking is described without saying whether it is good or bad.
Dialogue lines in a play is a neutral technical term.
The faculty of speaking is a plain name for a capacity, with no attitude.
Calling a person a success is favourable by definition, not by attitude beyond its meaning; it names an outcome rather than sneering or gushing.
Assembling for a common purpose is plain description; the sentences' coldness or warmth belongs to other words.
Joining together is described neutrally with no judgement of the joining.
A confluence of rivers is a plain geographic term.
Anything seen is neutral; 'odious' in the sentence does the judging, not 'sight'.
A visitor attraction is named plainly without saying whether it is worth seeing.
The act of seeing, as in 'out of sight', is plain description.
A range of mental vision is a neutral figurative extension with no attitude toward what is seen.
'A sight of' as a large amount is an informal intensifier; its register is casual but it takes no side on the thing quantified.
